primer.waf_p_world.title: Land of gold and salt
primer.waf_p_world.text: You were born in West Africa, in the savanna along the great River Niger. Here, between the desert and the rainforest, stand the richest kingdoms of their age: first Mali, then Songhai. Their strength lies in gold mined in the south, in salt carried by camel out of the Sahara, and in cavalry. Arab merchants call these lands Bilad al-Sudan, "the land of the Black peoples", and European maps show the local king holding a nugget of gold.
primer.waf_p_world_sundiata.title: The age of Sundiata
primer.waf_p_world_sundiata.text: Mali is just being born. According to the griots' songs, Sundiata Keita, a prince lame since childhood, united the Mandinka clans and around 1235 defeated Sumanguru, the fearsome sorcerer-king of Sosso, at Kirina. At the assembly of Kurukan Fuga, they say, he set the order of things – who fights, who rules, who works the crafts – though what was actually decided is known only from oral tradition. After Sundiata his sons and generals push the borders outward; for a time Mali was even ruled by Sakura, a former slave of the court.
primer.waf_p_world_musa.title: The gold of Mansa Musa
primer.waf_p_world_musa.text: Mali is at the height of its power, stretching from the Atlantic to the bend of the Niger. Mansa Musa, who ruled from about 1312 to 1337, set out on pilgrimage in 1324 with an enormous retinue and gave away so much gold in Cairo that its price there stayed low for years. He brought scholars and the architect al-Sahili back from Arabia, and the Djinguereber mosque rose in Timbuktu. His brother Mansa Suleyman rules until 1360; in 1352–1353 the traveller Ibn Battuta stayed at his court and marvelled at how safe the roads were.
primer.waf_p_world_decline.title: Mali in decline
primer.waf_p_world_decline.text: The great empire is weakening. The Keita family quarrel over the throne, mansas come and go quickly, and the outlying provinces fall away one by one. In 1433 Tuareg nomads took Timbuktu, Mossi horsemen raid from the south, and the Songhai of Gao stop paying tribute. Merchants tell of strange ships manned by white men off the ocean coast: the Portuguese have been appearing there since the 1440s. Mali still holds its old southern heartland, but a new power is rising on the Niger.
primer.waf_p_world_sonni.title: Sonni Ali
primer.waf_p_world_sonni.text: Gao is ruled by Sonni Ali Ber (1464–1492), one of the most formidable generals Africa has known. His cavalry and his fleet of river boats on the Niger almost never lose: in 1468 he drove the Tuareg out of Timbuktu, and around 1473, after a long siege, he took Djenne. The Muslim scholars of Timbuktu, whom he persecuted, remember him as a cruel tyrant, while folk legends make him a great magician who could turn into a bird. This is how the Songhai empire is born.
primer.waf_p_world_askia.title: The empire of the Askias
primer.waf_p_world_askia.text: Songhai is the largest state in West Africa. In 1493 the general Muhammad Ture seized power and took the title of askia. In 1496–1497 he made the pilgrimage, was named caliph of Takrur in Cairo, and on his return set governors over the provinces and became a patron of scholars. Under the Askias, Timbuktu and Djenne grow rich, while Gao remains the capital. The high point comes under Askia Dawud (1549–1582). But Morocco already has its eye on the salt mines of Taghaza.
primer.waf_p_world_morocco.title: Muskets across the desert
primer.waf_p_world_morocco.text: Songhai has fallen. The Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur, dreaming of the gold of the Sudan, sent Judar Pasha's army across the Sahara – about four thousand men, many armed with muskets. In March 1591, at Tondibi, gunfire scattered the huge army of Askia Ishaq II. The Moroccans occupied Gao, Timbuktu and Djenne, and in 1594 the scholar Ahmad Baba was carried off in chains to Marrakesh. The last Askias have retreated south to Dendi and fight on, while the arma soldiers lord it over the towns.
primer.waf_p_society.title: Clans and castes
primer.waf_p_society.text: At the top stands the ruler – the mansa in Mali, later the askia in Songhai – with his court. Society rests on the horon, the freeborn: farmers, warriors, merchants. Apart from them stand the nyamakala, hereditary specialists: blacksmiths, griot bards, leatherworkers. They are respected and a little feared, but nobody marries into their families. At the bottom are the jon, the enslaved: war captives and their descendants. A person's place is set by lineage, and a clan name – Keita, Traoré, Konaté – tells everyone at once where you belong.
primer.waf_p_society_slave.title: Jon
primer.waf_p_society_slave.text: You are one of the jon, the enslaved. Most were taken in wars and raids, for Mali and Songhai live partly by capturing people. Some work their masters' fields – the Askias have whole villages of slaves growing rice and millet for the court – others serve in households, and others are sold north across the Sahara. Custom frowns on selling those born in the household, who are treated almost as family. A slave can work his way up, and a few, like Sakura who ruled Mali, rose to the very top.
primer.waf_p_society_peasant.title: Free farmers
primer.waf_p_society_peasant.text: You come from horon farmers, free people. The family lives in a big compound under its senior man, and the village is led by the dugutigi, a descendant of the first settler who long ago made a pact with the spirit of the land. Before the rains everyone goes out with short-handled hoes to sow millet, sorghum and fonio; in the Niger delta they plant rice. Part of the harvest goes to the ruler, and in a drought people live off the stores in clay granaries. Work is done together, to a drumbeat – it goes faster and more cheerfully that way.
primer.waf_p_society_noble.title: At court
primer.waf_p_society_noble.text: You were born into a family close to the ruler's court. The nobility surround the mansa or the askia: generals, provincial governors called farba, counsellors, keepers of the treasury. Nobles wear silk and gold bracelets, ride costly horses from North Africa and own many slaves. The ruler rewards brave warriors with trousers: according to the Arab writer al-Umari, the wider the trousers, the greater the honour. But court is a dangerous place, where a word from the ruler can raise you up or ruin you in a single day.
primer.waf_p_birth.title: A name on the seventh day
primer.waf_p_birth.text: The older women of the family delivered you. A child is named on the seventh day: Muslim families shave the baby's head, slaughter a ram, and a learned man whispers the call to prayer into the baby's ear; among those who honour the ancestors the elders choose the name, often that of a grandparent, whose spirit is believed to have returned to the family. Until that day the baby is guarded from the evil eye and wicked spirits. The newborn is rubbed with shea butter, and a leather amulet is hung around its neck.
primer.waf_p_childhood.title: Children of one age
primer.waf_p_childhood.text: A mother carries her baby tied on her back with a length of cloth while she works the field or pounds millet in the mortar. From five or six, boys herd goats and chase birds from the crops, and girls carry water in calabashes and mind the little ones. Children of the same age grow up together as a group, a ton: they work and play together and later pass through the initiation into adulthood together. In the evenings by the fire the old people tell stories of the clever hare and the foolish hyena, and the griots sing of Sundiata.
primer.waf_p_childhood_islam.title: Quranic school
primer.waf_p_childhood_islam.text: In Muslim families boys are sent to Quranic school at about six. The teacher writes verses on a wooden board in soot ink; the pupil learns them by heart, washes them off and writes new ones. Lessons start at dawn, sitting on the sand outside the teacher's house, and he is paid in grain, firewood or cowrie shells. The brightest go on to Timbuktu or Djenne to spend years studying law and theology. Girls, too, sometimes learn a few suras by heart.
primer.waf_p_home.title: A clay compound
primer.waf_p_home.text: In the villages and in Niani people live in round mud houses with conical thatched roofs. Several of these huts – for the husband, for each wife, for cooking and for grain – stand together in a compound behind a mud wall. In the trading towns of Timbuktu and Djenne houses are square, built of mud brick, with flat roofs where people sleep on hot nights. Inside it is cool and dim: mats on the floor, water jars, calabashes and chests of cloth along the walls. After every rainy season the walls are given a fresh coat of mud.
primer.waf_p_food.title: Millet and kola
primer.waf_p_food.text: The staple is to, a thick porridge of millet or sorghum eaten with the right hand from a shared bowl, dipped in a sauce of baobab leaves or okra enriched with shea butter. In the Niger delta people eat rice; along the river, dried and smoked fish. Meat is for feast days, and milk and butter are bartered from Fulani herders. A guest is first offered kola nuts – bitter, stimulating and a sign of respect. And Saharan salt is so precious that it is used a pinch at a time.
primer.waf_p_clothes.title: Strips of cotton
primer.waf_p_clothes.text: Cloth here is woven by men on narrow looms, in strips a hand wide that are then sewn into broad lengths. It is dyed deep blue with indigo. Muslims wear loose boubou robes and turbans, and on Fridays, Ibn Battuta wrote, everyone puts on clean white clothes. The poor and children dress more simply, in a cotton wrap or skirt. The nobility glitter with gold bracelets and earrings and wear silk brought across the desert, while Tuareg men veil their faces with blue cloth.
primer.waf_p_faith.title: Two faiths side by side
primer.waf_p_faith.text: Two faiths live side by side here. Islam came across the Sahara with the merchants, and rulers, traders and the townsfolk of Timbuktu and Djenne hold to it. Most farmers honour the spirits of the land, the river and the ancestors, make offerings to them and wear amulets. The line between the two is soft: the mansa prays in the mosque yet still performs the ancient ancestral rites, and a village elder may wear a leather pouch holding a verse of the Quran. The closer you get to markets and mosques, the more Muslims you find; the deeper into the villages, the stronger the old faith.
primer.waf_p_faith_islam.title: Friday prayer
primer.waf_p_faith_islam.text: Your family is Muslim. There are five prayers a day, and on Fridays the congregational prayer in the mosque, which Ibn Battuta said was so crowded that servants spread their masters' mats in advance. In Ramadan people fast from dawn to dusk, and at the feast that ends the fast the whole neighbourhood gathers. The pilgrimage to Mecca is a journey of nearly a year; making it is a great honour, and everyone remembers Mansa Musa's example. Learned marabouts are revered, and people ask for their blessing.
primer.waf_p_faith_traditional.title: Nyama and the spirits
primer.waf_p_faith_traditional.text: Your family follows the faith of the ancestors. The world is full of nyama, a living force found in people, animals and trees, and above all in blacksmiths and hunters. Every village honours the guardian spirit of its land, and the river has spirits of its own, to whom fishermen bring gifts. Food and millet beer are left for the ancestors at the family shrine, and chickens are offered at crossroads. Men's secret societies such as the Komo, led by blacksmiths, keep the rites and judge sorcerers.
primer.waf_p_work.title: Caravans and cowries
primer.waf_p_work.text: Almost everyone grows millet, sorghum or rice, but the country's wealth is trade. From the north camel caravans bring slabs of salt from Taghaza, copper, cloth and books; from the south come gold from the Bambuk and Bure fields and kola nuts. People pay in cowrie shells brought from the distant Maldives, in gold dust and in bars of salt. Wangara merchants travel from market to market, blacksmiths forge hoes and arrowheads, and weavers, potters and fishermen sell their wares on market days.
primer.waf_p_place.title: Lands of the Niger
primer.waf_p_place.text: Your land is the Western Sudan, as Arab geographers call it: a broad savanna between the Sahara and the rainforest, cut through by the Niger. The river first flows north-east towards the desert, then turns south-east, and the richest towns stand on its great bend. For half the year it is dry and the harmattan wind blows dust in from the desert; then the rains come and the river floods for hundreds of kilometres. Everywhere there are baobabs, millet fields and herds.
primer.waf_p_place_niani.title: The mansa's town
primer.waf_p_place_niani.text: Tradition makes Niani the mansa's capital on the Sankarani River, among hills and millet fields, though historians still argue over where Mali's chief city really stood. This is home to the Keita clan, Sundiata's descendants. The mansa receives his subjects seated beneath a silk canopy, and no one may address him directly – only through a griot herald – while those who come before him sprinkle dust on their heads as a mark of respect. Not far to the south lie the gold fields of Bure.
primer.waf_p_place_timbuktu.title: On the edge of the desert
primer.waf_p_place_timbuktu.text: Timbuktu stands where the Niger comes closest to the desert. Legend says the town began as a camp around a well kept by an old woman named Buktu. Caravans of camels, sometimes thousands strong, arrive with slabs of Saharan salt, while grain, gold and slaves come up from the river port of Kabara. Above the flat mud roofs rise the mosques of Djinguereber, Sankore and Sidi Yahya, with wooden beams jutting from their walls.
primer.waf_p_place_gao.title: City on the bend
primer.waf_p_place_gao.text: Gao is an ancient Songhai city on the broad Niger, right at its great bend. It is home to Sorko fishermen and boatmen, who hunt even hippopotamuses, to farmers, and to merchants who cross the desert from North Africa and Egypt. Under Mansa Musa the city submitted to Mali, but from 1464 it is the capital of the Songhai empire, with the ruler's palace and a great market. Around 1495 Askia Muhammad built himself a tomb here, a tall pyramid of mud.
primer.waf_p_place_djenne.title: An island in the flood
primer.waf_p_place_djenne.text: Djenne stands on an island among the channels of the Bani River, and every year the flood turns the surrounding land into a lake, so that the town can be reached only by boat. Tradition says its ruler Koi Konboro embraced Islam in the thirteenth century and turned his palace into a mosque. Desert salt and gold, kola nuts and copper all meet here, and Wangara merchants carry goods on to the south. Nearby lie the ruins of Jenne-Jeno, a city more than fifteen hundred years old.
primer.waf_p_law.title: The mansa's justice
primer.waf_p_law.text: The highest judge is the ruler himself: Ibn Battuta watched the mansa hear complaints seated on a platform in his palace courtyard. In the trading towns disputes go to the qadi, a Muslim judge following the Maliki school. In the villages elders judge by ancestral custom, and secret societies deal with sorcery and grave offences. Punishments are harsh: a thief may be sold into slavery. Yet, the same traveller wrote, the roads are so safe that a man can travel alone with all his goods.
primer.waf_p_health.title: Fevers and amulets
primer.waf_p_health.text: The worst enemies here are malaria and the fevers of the rainy season, guinea worm from stagnant water, smallpox, and sleeping sickness near the rivers. Healers treat the sick with herbs, bark and roots and know hundreds of plants. Marabouts write Quranic verses on a board, wash the ink off with water and give it to the patient to drink, and they sew prayers into leather gris-gris amulets. Many children never reach adulthood. The dead are buried the same day; Muslims are wrapped in a white shroud and laid facing Mecca.
primer.waf_p_women.title: Women in plain sight
primer.waf_p_women.text: Women here are very much in public view: Ibn Battuta wrote indignantly that wives did not veil their faces, talked freely with men and went visiting friends. Girls marry young, and the groom's family pays a bride-price to hers; many men have two or three wives, each with her own hut and hearth. Women pound millet, cook, spin cotton, make pottery, trade in the markets and build up property of their own. In the epic of Sundiata one of the central figures is his mother Sogolon, plain-looking and wise.
primer.waf_p_leisure.title: Balafon and griots
primer.waf_p_leisure.text: The great entertainment is words and music. Griots, the jeli, sing of heroes to the ring of the balafon – a wooden xylophone with gourd resonators – and the strings of the ngoni, reciting their listeners' ancestors and receiving generous gifts. At court festivals, Ibn Battuta wrote, griots performed in bird masks. People celebrate harvests, weddings and initiations, and Muslims the end of the fast. They dance to drums, wrestle, race horses and spend evenings trading riddles.
primer.waf_p_knowledge.title: Book and memory
primer.waf_p_knowledge.text: Knowledge lives here in two forms. Arabic writing came with Islam and is used for letters, contracts, chronicles and books of law, while Timbuktu and Djenne build up libraries. But the people's memory is kept by the griots, the jeli, who pass down genealogies, customs and the epic of Sundiata by heart from generation to generation. Blacksmiths and hunters guard secret knowledge of their own, of metal, herbs and animals. Most people cannot read, yet they remember more than could ever be written down.
primer.waf_p_knowledge_timbuktu.title: City of books
primer.waf_p_knowledge_timbuktu.text: Timbuktu is a city of books. At the Sankore mosque and in scholars' homes young men spend years studying the Quran, law, grammar, astronomy and medicine; some come all the way from North Africa. They say manuscripts sell here at a better profit than any other goods, and a copyist can feed a family with his pen. Generation after generation, the Aqit family gives the city its qadis and teachers. Houses keep chests of leather-bound books, and a family's wealth is measured not only in gold but in its library.
primer.waf_p_war.title: Horsemen and archers
primer.waf_p_war.text: The strength of these kingdoms is cavalry: thoroughbred horses are brought from North Africa at great cost, and a horseman in mail or quilted armour is a man of rank. The bulk of the army is foot archers with poisoned arrows and spearmen from the villages. Al-Umari heard that the mansa's army numbered a hundred thousand; that is probably an exaggeration, but the army is truly enormous. The enemies are the Mossi to the south, the desert Tuareg and rebellious neighbours, and wars bring captives who are made slaves.
primer.waf_p_war_songhai.title: A fleet on the Niger
primer.waf_p_war_songhai.text: Songhai fights differently from old Mali: Sonni Ali and the Askias keep a standing army, not just a levy. There is cavalry in quilted armour, there are archers, and above all there is a fleet of long boats on the Niger crewed by Sorko fishermen, turning the river into a highway for the army. Campaigns go against the Mossi, the Tuareg, the Hausa lands and what remains of Mali. The Songhai have no firearms, and few here give a thought to the fact that beyond the desert men already fight with muskets.
